planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or bulbils in spring in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; sisal is nearly always propagated from the small plantlets (bulbils) that form on its flower stalk or from basal offsets rather than seed, since flowering plants are typically sterile hybrids.

directions: Sisal is a large, spineless-leaved agave historically cultivated across the world's tropics and subtropics as the source of sisal fiber, extracted from the long, rigid, blue-green leaves for rope, twine, and woven goods. In the garden it is grown mainly as a bold architectural accent, forming a rosette of stiff, sword-like leaves 3-5 feet long that tolerate salt spray, drought, and poor soil, making it a striking, near-maintenance-free specimen for a hot, dry, full-sun bed along the Gulf Coast. After many years a mature rosette sends up a dramatic branched flower stalk 15-20 feet tall studded with small bulbils, then the parent rosette dies, so plan for a succession of offsets to keep a planting going. It is not reliably frost-hardy and should be grown in a protected microclimate or container north of zone 9.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Nick or soak seed to soften the hard coat, then direct-sow or start in deep pots in spring in loose, deep, well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun; the long taproot resents transplanting and disturbance, so deep containers or direct seeding give the best results.

directions: Astragalus is a long-lived perennial legume grown for its pale, fibrous taproot, dried and sliced into the flat, tongue-depressor-shaped root known in traditional Chinese herbalism as huang qi, one of the most widely used tonic herbs in that tradition. The plant itself is an airy, pea-family perennial with ferny, pinnately compound leaves and small pale-yellow flowers in early summer, useful as a low-key border filler and pollinator plant as it slowly builds root mass over three or more growing seasons before harvest. It prefers lean, deep, well-drained soil and full sun and, like most deep-rooted legumes, is very drought-tolerant once established but does poorly in heavy, poorly drained clay. Roots are traditionally harvested in fall after the third or fourth year of growth, once they have reached pencil-to-finger thickness.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Scentlandia's compact, dense habit needs little pruning and works well massed along a shaded walkway where its fragrance can be appreciated up close.

directions: Scentlandia is a compact Southern Living Plant Collection selection of native Virginia sweetspire bred for noticeably stronger fragrance than older cultivars, packing dense, drooping, bottlebrush-shaped white flower spikes in early summer that perfume the air around a patio or walkway far more than the species. It stays low and mounded, well under 3 feet, with glossy summer foliage that turns burgundy in fall, and like other Itea selections it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil far better than most flowering shrubs. Give it moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; it flowers and colors well even in a fairly shaded spot, making it a good fit for a small, fragrant shade bed in the Gulf South.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Merlot Virginia Sweetspire (Compact Wine-Red Fall Color Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained to wet, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Merlot's compact, tidy habit needs little pruning beyond removing spent flower spikes and stays in bounds in smaller beds better than older, more vigorously suckering Itea cultivars.

directions: Merlot is a compact, rounded selection of native Virginia sweetspire bred to fit smaller gardens than older cultivars like Henry's Garnet, staying under 3 feet tall and wide while still producing the drooping, fragrant, bottlebrush-shaped white flower spikes of early summer that draw bees and butterflies. Its namesake feature is fall color that turns a deep wine-red to burgundy earlier and holds longer than most Itea selections, giving reliable color even in the mild autumns of zone 9. Like other Virginia sweetspire cultivars it tolerates wet, periodically flooded soil far better than most shrubs and develops good fall color even in partial shade, making it a useful, well-behaved choice for a rain garden edge or a shaded foundation bed where space is limited.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Halley's Comet Florida Anise (Large-Flowered Red Anise Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade in spring or fall; Halley's Comet flowers more heavily than the wild species and benefits from consistent soil moisture during its spring bloom period.

directions: Halley's Comet is a selection of native Florida anise chosen for producing a much heavier crop of flowers than typical seedling plants, with numerous, larger, deep maroon-red, multi-petaled starfish-shaped blooms that open along the branches in spring. Like the species it forms a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub with anise-scented foliage when bruised, thrives in the deep, acidic shade under pines and hardwoods that stumps many flowering shrubs, and is notably deer-resistant. Give it moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil and shelter from harsh afternoon sun, which can scorch the leaves; all parts of the plant are toxic if eaten and it should not be confused with the culinary star anise, Illicium verum.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
